title: Tech Layoffs Surge Past 150,000 in 2026 as AI Reshapes the American Workforce
excerpt: Meta, Amazon, Oracle, and Thomson Reuters lead a wave of cuts that has eliminated more jobs in six months than the full-year total in 2025, with software engineers bearing the brunt of AI-driven restructuring.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over 150,000 tech workers laid off in 2026, surpassing 2025's total with six months left.
  • AI drives layoffs while creating demand for specialized AI talent, leading to a divided job market.
  • Meta's layoffs of 8,000 employees sparked a lawsuit over AI's role in employment decisions.
  • Indian H-1B workers face a 60-day grace period to find new jobs after layoffs, complicating their situation.

  • More than 150,000 tech workers across 228 companies have been laid off in 2026, surpassing the full-year 2025 total of 246,000 with six months remaining.
  • AI is the primary driver: companies are simultaneously cutting traditional engineering roles while aggressively hiring AI-native talent, creating a bifurcated job market.
  • Meta alone cut 8,000 employees — 10% of its workforce — in May, with a lawsuit alleging its AI-powered ranking systems disproportionately targeted disabled workers.
  • Indian H-1B holders face a compounding crisis: layoffs trigger a 60-day grace period to find new sponsorship or leave the country.

The Scale of the Reckoning

The American tech industry is in the grip of its most severe workforce contraction since the post-pandemic correction of 2023, but this time the cause is structural rather than cyclical. According to the jobs tracker layoffs.fyi, more than 150,000 tech workers have lost their jobs across 228 companies in 2026. The website TrueUp estimates the year will end with 342,000 total cuts — a 39% increase over 2025's already painful 246,000.

The layoffs accelerated sharply in May, with mass dismissals at Meta, Oracle, LinkedIn, and Intuit. Thomson Reuters announced in July that it was eliminating up to 500 engineering jobs — roughly 5.2% of its technology workforce — as it aggressively deploys AI across its businesses.

"We are focusing our capacity where it matters most to customers," a Thomson Reuters spokesperson said, adding that the company plans to hire "more than 250 net-new engineering roles globally over the next two years, the large majority senior and AI-native."

The AI Paradox

The pattern is consistent across the industry: cut broadly, then hire narrowly. Companies are eliminating mid-level software engineering positions at scale while offering premium salaries to a small cohort of AI specialists. The result is a tech job market that looks simultaneously like a bloodbath and a gold rush, depending on your skill set.

The shift is driven by genuine productivity gains. AI coding assistants have advanced from intern-level capability to performing work equivalent to an engineer with two to three years of experience, according to Johan Mathe, founder of San Francisco-based AI weather forecasting company Atmo. "People started working so hard that they stopped sleeping," Mathe told Le Monde. "They were completely pale, with dark rings under their eyes. They were nicknamed the 'AI vampires.'"

"With this new model, it's as if we've gone from the level of a not-so-great intern to that of an engineer with two or three years of experience."

— Johan Mathe, Founder, Atmo

There is some consolation in the numbers. From January through May, 13,500 new tech hires were recorded — nearly triple the 5,500 over the same period in 2025. But the new hires are concentrated in AI and machine learning, offering little relief for the tens of thousands of web developers, QA engineers, and project managers whose roles are being automated.

The AI Ethics of Firing

Meta's May layoffs — 8,000 jobs, or 10% of its workforce — spawned a first-of-its-kind lawsuit that may define how AI can legally be used in employment decisions. Twenty-six anonymous plaintiffs allege that Meta used AI-powered ranking systems to target disabled workers and those on medical leave for termination.

According to the lawsuit, filed in Oakland federal court, Meta's internal tool "Metamate" — built on its Llama AI model — tracked employee productivity and tool usage. A separate system described as Meta's "second brain" monitored workers' typing, screen activity, and communications. The plaintiffs allege these systems penalized employees who missed work for health reasons, violating federal disability discrimination laws.

"The legal question won't be whether an employer used AI but whether it blindly trusted it," said Jon Hyman, chair of employment law at Wickens Herzer Panza.

The Indian Worker's Compounding Crisis

For Indian tech professionals in the United States — who constitute 4.3% of America's AI workforce and represent the single largest national group among H-1B visa holders — the layoffs carry consequences beyond unemployment. Under current rules, H-1B holders who lose their jobs have a 60-day grace period to find new employer sponsorship or leave the country. In a market where hundreds of applicants compete for every opening, that window is often insufficient.

The crisis is compounded by the Trump administration's recent $100,000 H-1B visa fee, which — though struck down by a federal judge on July 17 — created months of uncertainty and chilled employer willingness to sponsor new visa holders. Meanwhile, the proposed Duration of Status rule change, published July 17, would impose a four-year cap on student and certain work visas that previously had no fixed end date.

Together, these developments create a vise: fewer jobs available, more expensive to hire foreign workers, and shorter windows for those already here to remain legally.

What Comes Next

Industry analysts expect the pace of layoffs to moderate in the second half of 2026 as companies complete restructuring cycles. But the structural transformation is just beginning. As AI tools become more capable, the definition of "essential" engineering work will continue to narrow, and the workers who remain will be expected to produce dramatically more output with AI assistance.

For Indian tech workers weighing their options, the calculus is shifting. India's own startup ecosystem and its network of 2,100 Global Capability Centers — now employing 2.36 million people — offer an increasingly viable alternative to an American tech market that is simultaneously harder to enter, more expensive to navigate, and less stable than at any point in recent memory.
